answer.question: When was the move to three releases a year decided, and which release was the first to follow it?
answer.answer: The change was decided on April 23, 2021, when the Release Team merged the Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP-2572). It changed the release cycle from four releases a year (once a quarter) to three releases a year. The KEP set the new cadence to begin with the Kubernetes 1.22 release, using a 15-week release cycle with 2 weeks between cycles. 1.22 was also the KEP's alpha stage, a period focused on communicating the change. In practice, the project had already been running three releases a year since 2020, starting with 1.19. That year's 1.19 cycle was extended because of the COVID-19 pandemic, and 1.20 was the third and final release of 2020.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes move to three releases per year?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes moved from four releases a year (once a quarter) to three. A KEP making the change was merged on April 23, 2021. The reason given is that as the project matured, the number of enhancements per cycle grew. That added to the burden on contributors and the Release Engineering team. It also made it harder for end users, downstream consumers and integrators to keep up with increasingly feature-packed releases. Three releases a year balances these stakeholders' needs:

- **End users and integrators:** Many organizations found the old cadence hard to match. Each minor version now gets a longer support period, because the last three releases are supported and the longer cycles stretch that support. It also improves their ability to plan upgrades.
- **Contributors:** They get more time to mature enhancements and make them production-ready.
- **SIG Release / Release Engineering:** Management overhead drops, leaving more time for release quality and tooling. They maintain only 3 patch release streams instead of up to 4 overlapping ones. Handoffs between release teams can be smoother, and more shadows can be included.
- **Planning:** There is more room for triage, development, conferences and cycle preparation, so scheduling is more predictable.

answer.question: What enforces pod security standards in-tree?
answer.answer: The built-in Pod Security admission controller (Pod Security Admission) enforces the Pod Security Standards in-tree. It applies pod security restrictions at the namespace level when pods are created, and it can be configured with cluster-wide defaults and exemptions. It has been a built-in admission controller since v1.22. In v1.22 it needed the `PodSecurity` feature gate enabled; it was beta in v1.23 and became stable in v1.25. It replaces the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy. It can also be run as a standalone webhook.

answer.question: Why was PodSecurityPolicy replaced instead of fixed?
answer.answer:
PodSecurityPolicy had serious usability problems that couldn't be fixed without breaking changes, so it was deprecated (as of v1.21) rather than promoted to GA. The documented problems:

- **Confusing policy authorization model.** Policies were bound to either the requesting user or the pod's service account. Granting to the user was intuitive but broke controllers, and the dual model weakened security. It was also easy to accidentally grant broader permissions than intended, and hard to see which PSP(s) applied in a given situation.
- **Rollout challenges.** PSP failed closed when no policy existed, so it could never be enabled by default. You needed 100% coverage before rolling it out, and with no dry-run or audit mode it was impractical to retrofit to existing clusters safely.
- **Inconsistent and unbounded API.** The API grew organically and has many internal inconsistencies. It was unclear what belonged in PSP, it didn't compose well, mutation priority could be unexpected, and the "changing Pod defaults" feature only worked for some Pod settings, with no clear indication of when it applied.

The community still wanted a built-in way to prevent privilege escalation through the create-pod permission. So it built a replacement (KEP-2579, Pod Security Admission) designed around those lessons:
- It is as simple as practical, since external admission controllers (K-Rail, Kyverno, OPA/Gatekeeper) already cover advanced needs.
- It has soft rollout features so it can be retrofitted to existing clusters.
- It is configurable enough to eventually be on by default.
- It can be partially or fully deactivated to coexist with external controllers.

PSP was removed in v1.25.

answer.question: What happens to unused auto-generated ServiceAccount token Secrets?
answer.answer:
Since Kubernetes 1.29, the legacy ServiceAccount token cleaner in kube-controller-manager handles them in two steps: first it marks them invalid, and later it deletes them.

**When a Secret is marked invalid.** The cleaner runs every 24 hours. It checks the tracking ConfigMap created by the control plane, then evaluates Secrets of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`. It marks a Secret invalid when all of these are true:
- It is auto-generated, meaning it is bi-directionally referenced by a ServiceAccount.
- It is not mounted by any pod.
- It has not been used for a set period (one year by default).

**How the last-used date is determined.** The cleaner uses the `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-last-used` label if it exists and is after the `since` date in the `kube-apiserver-legacy-service-account-token-tracking` ConfigMap. Otherwise it uses `since`. If that ConfigMap is unavailable, no Secret is removed.

**How it is marked.** The cleaner adds the label `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-invalid-since`, with the current date as its value.

**If someone uses an invalidated token**, the validator:
- adds the audit annotation `authentication.k8s.io/legacy-token-invalidated`,
- increments `invalid_legacy_auto_token_uses_total`,
- updates the `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-last-used` label,
- returns an error saying the token has been invalidated.

Users can then remove the `invalid-since` label to temporarily re-enable the token, or switch to the TokenRequest API.

**When it is deleted.** If an invalidated token stays unused for another period (one year by default), the control plane deletes it.

Admins set both periods with `--legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period` on kube-controller-manager.

Earlier versions of the design (KEP drafts up to about 1.28) proposed deleting unused tokens directly after the period, with no invalidation step.

answer.question: Did Kubernetes create a token Secret for every ServiceAccount?
answer.answer: Yes, but only before version 1.24. Before 1.24, Kubernetes automatically generated Secret-based tokens for ServiceAccounts. These auto-generated Secrets are the ones referenced from the ServiceAccount's `secrets` field. In 1.24 the `LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration` feature gate went to beta and was enabled by default. With it enabled, Secret objects holding service account tokens are no longer auto-generated for every ServiceAccount. Instead, you get tokens through the TokenRequest API. If you need a non-expiring token, you can still explicitly create a Secret for the token controller to fill in, and an explicitly requested token is not deleted. From 1.29 onwards, legacy tokens that were auto-generated are marked invalid if they go unused for a set period (one year by default). If they stay unused for a further period of the same default length, the control plane purges them.

answer.question: When did legacy token cleanup reach GA?
answer.answer: The LegacyServiceAccountTokenCleanUp feature (from KEP-2799) reached GA (stable) in Kubernetes v1.30. Its path was alpha in 1.28 (off by default), beta in 1.29 (on by default), then stable in 1.30. Earlier versions of the KEP had planned GA for 1.26 and later 1.29, but it actually graduated in 1.30. The feature gate stayed stable through 1.31 and was then removed. The feature marks unused legacy secret-based service account tokens as invalid after one year by default, and deletes them if still unused after an additional year.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes stop auto-generating Secret-based ServiceAccount tokens?
answer.answer: Because once BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume went GA in 1.22, pods get their service account tokens through the TokenRequest API, stored as a projected volume. Those bound tokens are time-limited and tied to specific pods. That made auto-generating Secret-based tokens unnecessary, and the Secret-based tokens are less secure than the bound ones. Kubernetes therefore changed the Token Controller to stop auto-creating token Secrets for service accounts. This was the LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration feature: beta and on by default from 1.24, stable from 1.26. Users are pointed to the TokenRequest API, or to manually created Secret-based tokens if they need a non-expiring one. A related goal was to shrink the attack surface: the later LegacyServiceAccountTokenCleanUp feature marks unused auto-generated tokens invalid and eventually deletes them.

answer.question: Does the API server reject IP addresses with leading zeros by default?
answer.answer: It depends on the release. As of the latest release, yes. From 1.36 the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate is beta and enabled by default. With it enabled, the API server rejects IPv4 addresses whose octets have leading 0s, and also IPv4-mapped IPv6 values like ::ffff:192.168.0.1. In 1.33–1.35 the gate was alpha and disabled by default. In those releases such values were still accepted, but the API server returned a warning that they would be rejected in the future. Earlier, in 1.23, Kubernetes deliberately kept allowing leading zeros for compatibility and interpreted them as decimal. The stricter check applies only to fields in built-in API kinds. It does not apply to custom resources, Kubernetes configuration files or command-line arguments.

answer.question: Before strict IP validation was on by default, what happened when a Service used an IPv4 address with leading zeros?
answer.answer: The value was still accepted: Kubernetes kept allowing leading zeros in IPv4 addresses for compatibility, and it parsed them as decimal by ignoring the extra zeros (e.g. "012.000.001.002" was read as 12.0.1.2). Libc-based code may instead treat those octets as octal, which is the CVE-2021-29923 concern. Service IP/CIDR fields have also returned API server warnings for such values since 1.27. When the StrictIPCIDRValidation gate was off (alpha, off by default from 1.33 through 1.35), creating an object with such a value was allowed but produced a warning that it would be rejected in a future release. An example warning is: non-standard IP address "05.06.07.08" will be considered invalid in a future Kubernetes release: use "5.6.7.8". For instance, an invalid Service .spec.clusterIP is allowed with the gate disabled and causes an error with it enabled. From 1.36 the gate is beta and on by default.

answer.question: What are the release stages of strict IP/CIDR validation (KEP-4858)?
answer.answer:
Strict IP/CIDR validation is controlled by the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate.

- **Alpha:** Kubernetes 1.33 through 1.35, disabled by default. The KEP's Alpha criteria were:
  - API warnings added.
  - Mandatory strict validation for NetworkDeviceData.
  - All kube-internal controllers write out only canonical IPs/CIDRs.
  - Updated validation available behind the gate but disabled by default.
- **Beta:** from Kubernetes 1.36, enabled by default. The Beta criteria were:
  - UNRESOLVED items resolved.
  - Validation behind the gate, enabled by default.
  - Unit tests updated and old e2e tests removed.

  The KEP also required at least 3 releases between Alpha and Beta. This was so that components which might still write out invalid values (such as kubelet setting pod IPs from CRI/CNI) had been fixed to canonicalize them before the gate was turned on by default.
- **Stable:** the KEP document valid from 1.37 claims status implemented/stable and has a GA section in its Graduation Criteria. However, the feature gate reference provided lists only the alpha (1.33–1.35) and beta (1.36+) stages. The evidence does not give a GA release version.

evidence.section: KEP-4858: IP/CIDR Validation Improvements

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes tighten validation of IP addresses and CIDRs in API fields?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes' validation of IP addresses and CIDR strings in API fields had historically been too lax: it accepted any string the underlying Go functions (`net.ParseIP` and `net.ParseCIDR`) accepted. Some of those strings were ambiguous and could lead to security problems.

The concern is that different components may read the same string as different IP addresses, as in CVE-2021-29923. Two examples are IPv4 octets with leading `0`s and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values like `::ffff:192.168.0.1`.

After Go 1.17 changed how it handles leading-zero IPs to avoid that CVE, there was consensus that API validation should eventually become stricter too. This was not done right away, because the project didn't want to retroactively invalidate existing API objects. KEP-4858 set out the plan to finally do it.

The stated goal is to make ambiguously-interpretable IPs/CIDRs impossible in the future and so improve security. The 1.36 release post adds that stricter validation also catches malformed addresses and prefixes that previously slipped through. This helps prevent subtle configuration bugs that could cause confusing runtime behavior or security surprises.

The change was introduced as an alpha feature gate, `StrictIPCIDRValidation`, in 1.33 and graduated to beta (on by default) in 1.36. It applies only to built-in API kinds, not to custom resources, config files or command-line arguments.

It was rolled out cautiously. There were API warnings for several releases first, and the feature gate can be disabled. Pre-existing invalid values don't have to be fixed on unrelated updates. This was to reduce the risk of breaking existing clusters and automation.

answer.question: How long does a Kubernetes minor release receive patch support?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes 1.19 and newer get about 1 year of patch support. Kubernetes 1.18 and older got about 9 months.

The patch releases page gives the details. Under the yearly support KEP, a patch release series is supported for about 14 months:
- **First 12 months (standard period):** regular patch releases. Toward the end of this period, Release Managers cut a release and the series enters maintenance mode.
- **Next 2 months (maintenance mode):** Release Managers may cut extra releases only for:
  - vulnerabilities (CVEs), on the advice of the Security Response Committee
  - dependency issues, including base image updates
  - critical core component issues
- **End of life:** after maintenance mode, the series is EOL and cherry picks to its branch are closed soon after.

The 28th of the month is the target date for maintenance mode and EOL. The project keeps release branches for the three most recent minor releases.

heading_path: Why we decided to change the release cadence
What this means for end users

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes extend patch support for minor releases from 9 months to about a year?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes extended patch support mainly because end users asked for it. KEP-1498 explains the reasoning.

- **Annual business cycles:** Financial, certification, sales, vacation, HR and other business cycles are overwhelmingly annual. Many users wanted support that lasts at least a year. A 9-month window was an irregular period compared with how most companies plan, operate and budget.
- **Users were already falling behind:** A WG LTS survey in early 2019 found that a significant subset of users did not upgrade within 9 months. When 1.13 was current, about a third had production machines on 1.9 or 1.10, which were already out of support.
- **Expected improvement:** The survey suggested a 12–14 month window would let those users stay on supported versions. That would raise the share of users on supported versions from about 50–60% to more than 80%, whether they used DIY builds or vendor distributions.
- **Constant upgrade pressure:** With a new minor release every three months, users had to keep evaluating, planning and upgrading. They also had to track the deprecation and version skew policies.
- **A small, safe step:** The project saw the extension as a relatively minor change that was viable to implement and a meaningful first response to users. Keeping it small let them discover the unknowns of changing support windows.

The resulting policy is about 14 months: 12 months of standard support plus 2 months of upgrade or maintenance period. This formalized the existing practice of keeping patch-branch CI running for 6–7 weeks past the 9 months. It applies from 1.19 onward, which lets users adopt Kubernetes on an annual upgrade cycle.

Configuring the API Server using an authorization config file
Configuring the API Server using an authorization config file

answer.question: How do I configure the kube-apiserver to use more than one authorization webhook?
answer.answer:
Use a structured AuthorizationConfiguration file rather than the `--authorization-*` flags. With the flags you can only enable one webhook. The config file instead lists an ordered chain of authorizers, and you can include several entries of `type: Webhook`.

In the latest docs example the file uses `apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1` and `kind: AuthorizationConfiguration`. Older releases used v1alpha1 (1.29) and then v1beta1 (1.30–1.31).

Under `authorizers:`, give each authorizer a required `name`. A webhook entry has a `webhook:` block with these settings:
- `authorizedTTL` and `unauthorizedTTL`: how long responses are cached.
- `cacheAuthorizedRequests` and `cacheUnauthorizedRequests`: whether responses are cached at all (in the newest docs).
- `timeout`: required, with a maximum of 30s.
- `subjectAccessReviewVersion`: v1beta1 or v1.
- `matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion`: v1.
- `failurePolicy`: what happens when a webhook fails, returns a malformed response or errors evaluating conditions. `Deny` rejects the request without consulting later authorizers; `NoOpinion` continues to the next authorizer.
- `connectionInfo`: `type: KubeConfigFile` with a `kubeConfigFile` path (`KubeConfig` in older examples), or `InClusterConfig`. `InClusterConfig` is not allowed for kube-apiserver itself.
- Optional `matchConditions`: up to 64 CEL expressions. If any evaluates to false, the webhook is skipped. If all are true, it is called. On an error, `failurePolicy` decides the outcome.

Example shape:

```yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationConfiguration
authorizers:
  - type: Webhook
    name: webhook
    webhook:
      timeout: 3s
      subjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      failurePolicy: Deny
      connectionInfo:
        type: KubeConfigFile
        kubeConfigFile: /kube-system-authz-webhook.yaml
      matchConditions:
      - expression: has(request.resourceAttributes)
      - expression: request.resourceAttributes.namespace == 'kube-system'
  - type: Node
    name: node
  - type: RBAC
    name: rbac
  - type: Webhook
    name: in-cluster-authorizer
    webhook:
      timeout: 3s
      subjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      failurePolicy: NoOpinion
      connectionInfo:
        type: InClusterConfig
```

The evidence does not name the kube-apiserver flag that points at this file.

answer.question: What were the graduation stages of KMS v2 encryption at rest?
answer.answer:
The KMSv2 feature gate, which enables the KMS v2 API for encryption at rest, went through three stages:
- **Alpha:** releases 1.25–1.26, disabled by default.
- **Beta:** releases 1.27–1.28, enabled by default.
- **Stable (GA):** from 1.29, enabled by default.

The feature gate was later removed; the stable stage runs through 1.31.

As KMSv2 graduated, the KMSv1 gate was deprecated in 1.28 (still on by default). From 1.29 it is deprecated and off by default.

answer.question: When did ValidatingAdmissionPolicy go alpha, beta and GA?
answer.answer: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy went alpha in Kubernetes 1.26, where it stayed through 1.27 with the feature gate off by default. It became beta in 1.28, where it stayed through 1.29 and was still off by default. It reached GA (stable) in 1.30, with the gate on by default. The gate stayed stable through 1.31 and has since been removed. The 1.30 GA announcement blog post also confirms general availability in that release.

answer.question: Is kube-proxy's ipvs mode still supported, and what should I use instead?
answer.answer:
ipvs mode is still available, but it is deprecated. Kubernetes v1.35 deprecated it: the mode remains usable, and kube-proxy logs a deprecation warning on startup when configured with mode: ipvs.

The announced timeline:
- By v1.40, ipvs mode is expected to be disabled by default, though still selectable via a feature gate.
- By v1.43, ipvs support is expected to be removed entirely.

The KEP says the IPVS proxy will simply be removed from the tree, through a Deprecated feature gate, and not moved to a separate repository.

On Linux nodes, use nftables mode instead; it is the recommended replacement. The KEP notes that all kernels too old to support kube-proxy's nftables mode will be out of LTS by the end of 2026.

To check which mode you are running:
kubectl -n kube-system get configmap kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.conf}' | grep 'mode:'

The stated reasons for the deprecation are:
- Keeping feature parity between ipvs and the other modes created technical debt and complexity.
- The kernel ipvs API alone cannot fully implement Services, so ipvs mode still relies on iptables underneath.

answer.question: Should a new controller watch Endpoints or EndpointSlices to find a Service's backends?
answer.answer:
Watch EndpointSlices, not Endpoints. As of Kubernetes 1.33 the v1 Endpoints API is officially deprecated, and the API server returns warnings when you read or write Endpoints. Newer Service features are only available through EndpointSlice. These include dual-stack, traffic distribution/topology, and Services with more than 1000 endpoints. An Endpoints object shows only the cluster's primary address family. Service proxies, Gateway API implementations and kube-proxy have all moved to EndpointSlices.

There is also a plan to let clusters run without the Endpoints controller. KEP-4974 aims to change the conformance criteria so that clusters no longer have to run the Endpoints and EndpointSlice Mirroring controllers. Disabling them is meant to become a supported, conforming setup, so a controller that relies on Endpoints may find no objects at all.

When consuming EndpointSlices, don't assume one object per Service the way Endpoints works. List them with the label selector `kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>`. A Service can have several slices: separate ones for IPv4 and IPv6, separate ones when endpoints target different ports (for example during a rollout), and multiple slices once a Service has more than 100 endpoints.

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how did you turn on IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking?
answer.answer:
In 1.20 you turned it on by enabling the `IPv6DualStack` feature gate on the relevant cluster components and setting dual-stack network assignments:

- kube-apiserver: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`
- kube-controller-manager: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`, `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`. `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4` / `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6` default to /24 for IPv4 and /64 for IPv6.
- kubelet: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`
- kube-proxy: `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`

Once dual-stack was enabled, you could create Services that use IPv4, IPv6, or both, and change this setting on existing Services. In 1.20 this was a reimplementation that was expected to progress from alpha to beta and GA. Starting in 1.21 the gate defaulted to enabled.

answer.question: When did kube-proxy's nftables mode become generally available, and what came before?
answer.answer:
The nftables mode for kube-proxy became generally available (stable) in Kubernetes v1.33. Even at GA, iptables stays the default proxy mode on Linux nodes for compatibility reasons.

The path to GA was:
- **Alpha (v1.29):** The KEP-3866 proposal was first written on 2023-02-01 and merged on 2023-10-06. In the 1.29 changelog the mode was described as functionally mostly identical to iptables mode, with some differences:
  - It does not support NodePorts on 127.0.0.1.
  - It has no nftables-specific command-line flags, so those settings need a config file.
  - It had not yet been optimized or performance-tested much.
- **Beta (v1.31):** It moved to beta behind the `NFTablesProxyMode` feature gate, which was enabled by default. The KEP was updated for beta on 2024-05-24. At this stage:
  - It was Linux-only and required kernel 5.13 or later.
  - It might not work with all network plugins.
  - Some NodePort behaviors differed from iptables mode.
- **GA (v1.33):** The KEP was updated for GA on 2025-01-15. The GA criteria required at least two releases since beta, non-trivial real-world usage, and no bugs serious enough to hold back recommending it.

A later proposal, KEP-5343 (provisional, alpha), plans to make nftables the default proxy mode at its GA in 1.40.

answer.question: How did support for multiple Service CIDRs (ServiceCIDR objects) progress through its release stages?
answer.answer:
Multiple Service CIDRs (KEP-1880) is controlled by the MultiCIDRServiceAllocator feature gate, which tracks Service cluster IP allocations using IPAddress objects. It progressed as follows:

- **Alpha, 1.27–1.30:** disabled by default.
- **Beta, 1.31–1.32:** still disabled by default.
- **Stable (GA), from 1.33:** enabled by default and locked.

The KEP's implementation history lists the alpha and beta KEP, code and docs PRs, plus the stable-stage KEP and code PRs. The KEP's beta graduation criteria included:
- API stability (ServiceCIDR immutability, default IPFamily, one or two IP families per ServiceCIDR)
- user feedback
- more complex testing
- scale testing to O(10K) services and O(1K) ranges
- O(1) allocation performance

For GA, the KEP cites real-world usage:
- available in GKE since 1.31 and used in production clusters
- community testing since it went beta in 1.31
- only one bug reported

An earlier version of the KEP (valid 1.30–1.32) planned the following path:
- 1.32: beta, enabled
- 1.33: GA
- 1.34: GA with no bitmaps running, alongside a DisableAllocatorDualWrite gate
- 1.35: feature gates removed

However, the feature gate reference shows beta remained off by default through 1.32.

answer.question: Why did SIG Network build a new nftables backend for kube-proxy?
answer.answer:
Per KEP-3866 and the v1.29 release blog, the motivations were:

- **iptables has hit its limits.** iptables was the preferred Linux packet-filtering system for many years. Unsolvable problems with it, including performance problems the KEP calls unfixable, led to its successor, nftables. Development on iptables has mostly stopped, and new features and performance work go into nftables instead.
- **iptables is being removed from distributions.** Some Linux distributions have already started to deprecate and remove iptables, and nftables claims to solve iptables' main performance problems.
- **Neither existing workaround is enough.** The KEP's motivation section includes "the ipvs mode of kube-proxy will not save us" and "the nf_tables mode of /sbin/iptables will not save us". It also says the iptables mode has grown crufty.
- **One backend instead of two.** SIG Network currently supports both the iptables and ipvs backends. It feels it can't drop ipvs because of perceived performance issues with iptables. A new backend that is as functional and non-buggy as iptables but as fast as ipvs could eventually let both be deprecated, leaving one Linux backend to support.
- **A focus for cleanup.** Writing a new mode is expected to focus cleanup and refactoring of the kube-proxy "library" code.
